title: The Linux filesystem
summary: Explore a safe simulated root and connect /, /home, /etc, /var, /tmp, /usr, and /bin with their common Linux filesystem roles.

content.objective: Use read-only commands and relative paths inside a safe simulated root to identify the filesystem root and explain the common roles of /home, /etc, /var, /tmp, /usr, and /bin.
content.instructions: Inspect only the supplied simulated-root fixture. List its modeled root-level directories, then read the role cards in the requested order. Use paths beginning with simulated-root/, never inspect the sandbox's real /, and do not create, edit, move, or remove anything.

fixtures.content:
SAFE MODEL ONLY
simulated-root represents the Linux filesystem root /.
Inspect only this fixture with read-only commands.
/home: personal directories and files for users
A user's personal note belongs in the user's home directory.
/var: changing data such as logs, queues, and caches
/tmp: short-lived working files that may be removed
Temporary practice data; do not depend on it for long-term storage.
/usr: installed programs, libraries, and shared data
/bin: basic command programs; often linked into /usr on modern systems
This text label represents a basic command program.

tasks.title: Survey the simulated root
tasks.instructions: Run ls simulated-root. Treat the listed home, etc, var, tmp, usr, and bin directories as safe models of directories immediately below /. The simulated-root directory is not the real filesystem root.

tasks.title: Identify personal user space
tasks.instructions: Use cat with the relative path simulated-root/home/ROLE.txt. Read how /home commonly organizes users' personal directories and files.

tasks.title: Contrast configuration, changing data, and temporary data
tasks.instructions: In one cat command, read these three relative paths in exactly this order: simulated-root/etc/ROLE.txt, simulated-root/var/ROLE.txt, simulated-root/tmp/ROLE.txt. Contrast system-wide settings, changing operational data, and short-lived working files.

tasks.title: Contrast installed resources and basic commands
tasks.instructions: In one cat command, read simulated-root/usr/ROLE.txt and simulated-root/bin/ROLE.txt in that order. Connect /usr with installed programs, libraries, and shared data, and /bin with basic command programs.

hints.text: Use the read-only listing command with the fixture directory's relative name. Do not add a leading /, because / is the sandbox's actual filesystem root.
The command is ls and its one argument is simulated-root. Look for six directory names in the output.
Use the short-text reading command with a relative path through simulated-root, then home, then ROLE.txt.
Use cat. The required path begins simulated-root/home/ and ends with ROLE.txt.
One cat command can accept several file arguments. Keep the requested order: configuration first, changing data second, temporary data third.
After cat, provide the ROLE.txt paths under etc, var, and tmp, each beginning with simulated-root/.
Use one read-only cat command for the two remaining role cards. Read the broader installed-resource role before the basic-command role.
The ordered paths are the ROLE.txt files under simulated-root/usr and simulated-root/bin.

tutor.goalSummary: Student safely inspects a simulated root, identifies / as the top of the Linux filesystem tree, and accurately contrasts the common roles of /home, /etc, /var, /tmp, /usr, and /bin.
misconceptions: simulated-root is an ordinary fixture directory that models selected children of /; it is not the sandbox's real filesystem root.
The filesystem root / is a directory and is distinct from the administrative user account named root.
/home commonly holds users' personal directories, whereas /etc commonly holds system-wide configuration.
/var refers to changing operational data such as logs, not storage for shell variables.
/tmp is for short-lived work and should not be assumed permanent or automatically private.
/usr commonly holds installed programs, libraries, and shared data; it is not one user's personal home.
/bin has the traditional role of basic command programs, although modern systems often link it into /usr.
Directory roles are conventions and do not grant permission to inspect or alter a real system.
constraints: Keep all terminal coaching inside workspace/simulated-root and use only workspace-relative fixture paths beginning with simulated-root/.
Never suggest cd /, ls /, cat with an absolute system path, or any exploration of the sandbox or host root.
Use only read-only ls and cat commands; do not suggest commands that create, edit, copy, move, rename, change permissions, or delete entries.
Give each task's hints in level order, ask the student to predict the directory role first, and reveal the exact command only at level 3.
Do not provide all four commands as a pasteable sequence or complete later tasks for the student.
Describe these roles as common Linux conventions and acknowledge distribution differences, especially the modern relationship between /bin and /usr.
After completion, ask the student to place a personal document, system setting, changing log, and disposable scratch file into /home, /etc, /var, and /tmp with reasons.
Require the student to explain why simulated-root is safe practice rather than the real /.
